content_preview.title: Google Reports Unprompted Detours to TODO Bug References Added 70% More Steps and 77% More Tokens per Session in Its Agent Traces
content_preview.summary: Google's developer blog says agents ignored inline TODO bug references in 94% of encounters, and that unprompted detours to them added 70% more steps per session.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A [Google Developers Blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/agent-distraction/) post dated November 6, 2026 reports that AI coding agents sometimes act on inline `TODO(bug/...)` comments in the code they read, including some tied to bugs that are already closed, and that unprompted detours of this kind made the affected sessions longer and costlier. The post is by Sam Saccone, a senior staff software engineer, and Madhuri Garikapati, a senior staff data scientist. It frames the pro...

editor_notes.content_quality: Compact 710-word Briefing with the right structure (what Google measured, what the traces showed, cost, what Google did, what the sources do not say). Figures are labelled as Google's, the Herald states no figure of its own, and the closing section names the gaps (no baselines, no agent or model named, no outside measurement, TODO/FIXME scope only, InfoQ restates the post).
editor_notes.source_verification: Snapshots read from disk (gunzip + text extraction): source-0.html.gz (developers.googleblog.com/agent-distraction/, HTTP 200, sha256 c291a715...e1741) and source-1.html.gz (infoq.com/news/2026/11/google-agent-distraction/, HTTP 200, sha256 ecaccae0...e7c6). Both hashes re-verified after decompression against manifest.json. Both URLs were also fetched live with curl and a browser User-Agent as raw HTML: the Google post came back byte-identical in size (43418) and contained the same 94%, 83% sessions, 70% more steps and exceeding 95% strings; the InfoQ page is dynamic (198014 vs 197992 bytes) with identical article text. No Archive.org fallback needed. suspicious_patterns is null for both sources. Source 0 (Google Developers Blog, Nov. 6, 2026, Saccone and Garikapati) confirms every figure in the article: 13% of file-reading sessions exposed to TODO/FIXME(bug/...); 94% ignored 'in encounters'; 6% took action targeting the bug ID; 83% unprompted; 41% closed (32% fixed/verified + 9% obsolete/won't-fix) plus 2% duplicate/restricted; 57% open with 61% lookup only and 39% edited code (41+2+57 = 100, consistent); regression controls and p<0.0001; 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, 105% more wait time; SurfaceControlTest.java bug fixed in 2023; ModelDownloaderV1 and human challenge of scope creep; 'only trivial to minor detours'; todo cleaner, thousands removed over six months, 'exceeding 95% acceptance from human reviewers'. Direct quotes ('What is easy for humans to skim past...', 'provide the perfect proxy', 'tend to be left behind long after...', 'todo cleaner', 'exceeding 95%') are verbatim. Source 1 (InfoQ, Sergio De Simone, Nov 10, 2026) confirms the publication date, the 'approximately 13%' and 'in 6% of those cases' wording (quoted verbatim in the article), 41%/57%, 70%/77%/105%, and the Tulasiram quote; InfoQ also relays three other reactions (Ryan White, Awais Raza, Muhammad Zohaib) that the article does not mention, which is a choice, not an error. Neither source names the agent or model, gives baseline step/token/time counts, or reports a measurement outside Google, as the article says. Independence: 1 independent outlet (InfoQ), and it restates the post; the article says so itself. Briefing minimum is 2 sources. Allowlist: infoq.com (line 197) and developers.googleblog.com (line 843) are listed; no additions. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Google, its developer blog and InfoQ are the only parties; no Anthropic or Claude product is a subject, a figure, or a credit line (grep for anthropic/claude in the body returns 0).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Claim-accuracy tests run from raw text. (1) Absence and quantifier sentences: 'neither cited source names the agent or the model', 'neither gives the baseline ... counts', 'or reports a measurement from outside Google' hold against both snapshots; 'the agent only looked the issue up in 61%' is the post's '61% lookup only'; 'both' and 'only trivial to minor detours' match the post. (2) Headline, summary, lead: the title and summary attribute to Google, keep 'per Session' and 'in Its Agent Traces', use 'encounters' for the 94% as the post does, and do not name an agent or imply a cause beyond Google's own regression framing. The summary's 70% is correctly 'per session' and sourced to Google. The one soft spot is the lead's 'made the affected sessions longer and costlier': the post says only 'Per session', so 'affected sessions' is the writer's reading. (3) Dates: Nov. 6 (post) and Nov 10 (InfoQ) match; no time zone is given by either and none is claimed. (4) Derived figures: the article states no Herald-computed figures; 41+2+57 reconciles to 100. (5) Disagreements between sources: the 94%-of-encounters vs InfoQ's '6% of those cases' (sessions exposed) wording is reported with both attributions and left unreconciled, which is the honest handling. Additional unit gap the article does not flag: the post writes 'Over 4 in 5 of those actions (83% sessions)', mixing actions and sessions, and the article reports 'actions' without noting the post's own '(83% sessions)' wording. (6) Independence recounted: one independent outlet, restating the post. Minor paraphrase: the post says the agents looked at 'changes to the codebase', the article says 'related changes'.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; vendor claims attributed throughout; no editorializing; the only reaction quoted is attributed to a named InfoQ-cited user.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. No existing article or submission matches the Agent Distraction post (grep for 'TODO(bug', 'agent distraction' across articles and submissions found only this submission). Closest recent coverage (Glow Labs on coding agents and archived MCP servers, 2026-11/07; where coding agents leave secrets, 2026-11/08) concerns different findings.
concerns: The post's '(83% sessions)' parenthetical mixes a session unit into an action share; the article reports 'actions' without flagging the ambiguity it flags for 94%/6%.

The post does not say what the 70%/77%/105% increases are measured against, and the lead calls them an increase for 'the affected sessions'; the closing section names missing baseline counts but not the missing comparison group.
Single first-party source of data; the only independent outlet restates it. Disclosed in the article, so not a defect.
recommendations: File a clarification record covering the 83% unit and the unspecified comparison group for the percentage increases; both are incomplete rather than wrong, and neither touches the headline's attribution or figures.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-hedged Briefing: every figure, quote and date traces to the Google post or InfoQ, the unit ambiguities that matter most (94% encounters vs 6% of cases) and the absent baselines are disclosed, and title, summary and lead keep Google's attribution and the per-session qualifier. Two incomplete (not wrong) subordinate points justify an APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS clarification record. Featured candidacy: 1 - useful, quantified vendor measurement for teams running coding agents, but a single first-party dataset with unspecified baselines
